Tonight, in one sentence

You watch a model get revised, hold your own finding up against your model, and learn the difference between a model that explains and one that predicts.

A finding that can’t tell is not a failure. It is a request for a better design.

The loop

In Module 1, Box described learning as a loop:

the model says what to look for, the data pushes back, the model improves.

Your preliminary finding is the data pushing back. Tonight a real project goes around the loop once, where you can watch every step.

Where the Results draft stands

  1. The question and the prediction
  2. The chart
  3. The association
  4. How it compares with your model
  5. What it does not establish

Tonight builds sections 2 through 4, and starts section 5.

Due before your Module 3 kick-off: Tue Nov 17, 6:00 pm (Salem) or Wed Nov 18, 6:00 pm (Portland). Thursday’s session is the work session.

Gallery

6:10 to 6:25 · whole room, nobody moves

Fernhill, in thirty seconds

  • A fictional software firm: about 1,100 engineers in 120 product teams.
  • In July 2025 it reorganizes in all 120 teams at once: hire professional managers on people skill, make the old engineer-managers technical leads, and let AI fill the manager’s technical gaps.
  • Delivery is the share of a team’s committed milestones delivered by their dates.
  • One project, developed in the open in three versions alongside yours. Tonight: version 1’s first analysis, and what Fernhill did next.

robertwwalker.github.io/Integrated622/fernhill/

How the gallery works

Three notes on each chart, alone, on paper, 90 seconds a chart:

  1. The question. What question does this chart answer?
  2. The answer. What does it say the answer is?
  3. The limit. What can’t it tell me?

Then a few of you read yours aloud, and we compare with what Fernhill meant.

These are Fernhill’s charts, not yours. Say what you read, not what you hope.

Chart 1

Chart 1: what Fernhill meant

This chart answers: how did delivery move, quarter by quarter, before and after the reorganization?

Delivery is a measurement (a share), and the quarter is a date. Each dot is one team in one quarter, 120 a quarter. The solid line joins the quarterly medians and the dashed line joins the quarterly averages. The dotted lines join the 25th and 75th percentiles, with a quarter of teams below the first and a quarter above the second.

What it can’t tell me, in the draft’s own words:

At the average, the fall is weak. Every after-quarter (61.4% to 67.8%) sits inside the range of the before-quarters (61.4% to 70.3%).

Chart 2

Chart 2: what Fernhill meant

This chart answers: how is delivery spread across team-quarters before and after July 2025, and where do the average, the median and the most common band fall?

Delivery is a measurement (a share). Each bar is the share of that period’s team-quarters in a ten-point band (960 before, 480 after). The dashed line marks the average, the solid line marks the median, and the darkest bar marks the most common band.

What it can’t tell me, in the draft’s own words:

The three measures disagree because they answer different questions, and they agree only when a distribution is symmetric.

Chart 3

Chart 3: what Fernhill meant

This chart answers: what else changed in July 2025?

Each point on a line is one quarter, averaged over the 120 teams. The first two panels plot the share of teams with a professional manager (from a label) and with AI licenses (from a yes/no), and the third plots milestones committed per team (from a count).

What it can’t tell me, in the draft’s own words:

In all 1,440 team-quarters a professional manager and AI licenses go together, 480 with both and 960 with neither. The third chart’s first two panels are the same line.

Your own chart

Do the same three notes on your chart when you work later tonight:

  1. What question does it answer?
  2. What does it say?
  3. What can’t it tell me?

Want a pod-mate’s notes too? Post the chart to your pod’s thread. That is the pod’s part, and it happens on the board.

Fernhill: a model, revised

6:25 to 7:10 · version 1, then version 2

Version 1: the model and the prediction

The model. People skill lowers coordination friction. AI covers the manager’s technical gaps. Technical judgment stays with the lead, so nothing technical is lost. In short, the reorganization puts people skill in the manager’s chair without losing technical judgment, so delivery rises.

The prediction, stated before looking:

  • Delivery rises after July 2025, by about 5 percentage points, after a dip in the first quarter.
  • People-skill ratings rise.
  • The rise holds on hard quarters as well as easy ones.

The Brief didn’t say which summary of delivery the 5 points meant, so the Results draft reads it as the average.

Your call

The prediction: delivery up about 5 points, ratings up, the rise holding on hard quarters.

Finding Your verdict
Average delivery: 63.4% after, 65.3% before ?
People-skill ratings: 0.69 before, 0.79 after ?
Easy quarters 74.9% to 79.4%; hard quarters 52.8% to 41.0% ?
Median delivery: 68.2% before, 72.6% after ?

Consistent, inconsistent, or can’t tell yet? Hands, or the chat.

The verdicts

Finding Verdict
Average delivery, lower Inconsistent. The model said up about 5 points, though the predicted first-quarter dip did appear (61.4% against 62.8%)
Ratings 0.69 to 0.79 The prediction holds. A honeymoon for new managers would predict the same rise, but it should fade, and this one held (0.78 to 0.80 in each of the four quarters after)
Hard quarters fell Inconsistent, but can’t tell yet. Difficulty was rated after the outcome, so it may be an artifact
Median, up 4.4 points Consistent, but not a pass. The reading was chosen after the average failed, and AI alone would predict the same rise

The Brief’s own tests

The Brief said the model is wrong if:

At the average
1. Delivery is no higher after than before Holds
2. Ratings rise but delivery doesn’t Holds
3. Delivery rises on easy quarters but falls on hard Holds

It also said what had to be true for those tests to count:

“Nothing else that affects delivery may change at the same time.”

Did it hold?

Why it couldn’t tell

  1. Two changes at once. Professional managers and AI licenses arrived together.
  2. Something else changed at the same moment. The year’s customer migration.
  3. The hard-quarter test was circular. Difficulty was rated after the outcome.
  4. No comparison group. Every team changed, so the only baseline was the past.

Which of the four findings does each reason weaken?

Reason 1: two changes, one variable

In all 1,440 team-quarters Team-quarters
Professional manager and AI licenses 480
Neither 960
One without the other 0

In this data they are one variable, so any difference belongs to both, and nothing can split it.

Reason 2: something else changed

Before After
Milestones committed, per team-quarter 18.0 20.2
Milestones delivered, per team-quarter 11.6 12.8
Share delivered 65.3% 63.4%

Committed work was higher in 94 of 120 teams: the customer migration every team took on from July 2025.

Teams delivered more, but a smaller share of a bigger load. The Brief had assumed nothing else would change.

Reasons 3 and 4

Circular. Difficulty was rated at the quarter’s close, after the outcome. Quarters that delivered under 60% were rated hard 83% of the time, against 21% of the rest. A rating made afterward can’t separate “hard work went badly” from “work that went badly was called hard.”

No comparison group. Every team changed, so the only baseline was the past, and the past can’t absorb a change that hit the whole firm.

Noticed, not pursued

The file held records version 1’s model never asked about.

  • Escalations fell from 9.9 to 7.5 a team-quarter.
  • Lead departures rose from 3.6% to 11.9% of teams a quarter.
  • The spread widened: the weakest quarters got weaker while the middle improved.
  • We never asked IT what teams actually did. A license shows access, not use.

Whatever the model leaves out is where the next version comes from.

What we decided, and why

Decision Why
Separate the two changes into three groups, engineer-managers without AI, engineer-managers with AI, and professional managers with technical leads and AI Reason 1, so the reorganization and AI can be told apart
Assign the groups by lot, 40 teams each, and compare each group with its own eight quarters before Reasons 2 and 4, since a firm-wide change falls on every group alike, and the lot makes the groups comparable
Rate difficulty at the quarterly planning review, before the work Reason 3, since a rating made before the outcome can’t be bent by it
Ask IT for the usage logs A license says who could use AI, not who did, and a no-AI arm has to stay that way
Model where technical questions go, through escalations and the wait for an answer from whoever holds technical judgment Version 1’s claims that “AI covers the gaps” and “nothing technical is lost” couldn’t be checked against any record, and escalations were moving

How the analysis changed

What the lot buys

  • Each arm against its own past. A firm-wide change falls on every arm alike.
  • The lot makes the arms comparable. No one chose which teams got what.
  • The two changes come apart. AI alone, and the new structure with AI, can be seen separately.

A before-and-after can say what changed. A comparison by lot is what lets you say what the change did.

What changed in the Project Brief

Element Version 1 Version 2
What Fernhill does Adopts the plan everywhere, with AI at the same time Runs a one-year pilot by lot, three arms of 40
The model AI covers the manager’s gaps, and judgment stays with the lead Difficulty sets how many unknowns arrive, and AI clears only routine ones. Unknowns queue at whoever holds technical judgment, and the wait explodes near capacity
The method Before and after A randomized pilot

What didn’t change

Lines that didn’t change are word for word the same in both versions, so what changed is exactly what the new model required.

Every difference between version 1 and version 2 traces to a reason on the last few slides. Read it yourself on the Fernhill page, under What version 1 taught us.

Not wrong, incomplete

  • By its own rule, wrong at the average. All three of the Brief’s “wrong if” conditions held.
  • But its own assumption failed. “Nothing else may change” did not hold, so even the three failures may belong to the comparison.
  • So the honest verdict was “can’t tell yet,” and the Results draft said so.
  • Incomplete, not wrong. It couldn’t separate the two changes, rated difficulty after the outcome, and had no place for escalations, departures or usage.

A test is only as good as its assumptions.

And version 2?

A stronger test of the same model, with new pieces: a queue for technical questions, difficulty rated before the work, and IT’s usage logs.

It will have its own section 5, on what it doesn’t establish.

Thursday you will see what the trial found, and what it still leaves out.

Every model you build will be incomplete. The goal is to be able to say how.

Same move, a different case

Version 2 adds a queue to the model: near capacity, waits explode (Little’s Law). At Riverbend the prediction is: if referrals rise and staffing doesn’t, waits should rise too.

Where we look What the data say Your verdict
Month by month, all sites correlation 0.80 ?
Week to week, within a site correlation 0.07 ?
Where capacity fell (S1, S2) open positions up; waits? ?

Consistent, inconsistent, or can’t tell yet? Say it before the next slide.

Three verdicts, one model

  • Month by month: consistent. Referrals and median waits move together strongly (0.80). The winter surge brings the longest waits.
  • Week to week within a site: can’t tell yet. The correlation is near zero (0.07). A single busy week may not be enough to build a queue.
  • When capacity falls: consistent. At S1, open positions went from 0.8 to 1.8 on average and the median wait from 4.8 to 5.3 days. At S2, open positions went from 2.5 to 5.3 and the wait from 5.4 to 5.7.

The model held where its conditions held, and the data was silent where they didn’t. That is what an honest Results section sounds like.

Your verdict

Five minutes, alone, one sentence: the verdict on your own finding, and why.

Verdict Means What to write
Consistent The data looks the way your model predicted Consistent with the model, which is not the same as proving it. Name another model that would predict the same thing.
Inconsistent The data looks different from the prediction Which part of the model is wrong, or which way the data might be lying? This is often the most useful finding.
Can’t tell yet The data can’t separate your prediction from others What data, or what comparison, would let you tell?

The revision memo

Fifteen minutes, alone. Three lines, in Fernhill’s own form (a decision, and why):

Your line
What my finding can’t separate
The records I already have, or could get, that would
The smallest change to my design or model

Fernhill’s example: “Assign the groups by lot, 40 teams each” | “A firm-wide change falls on every group alike, and the lot makes the groups comparable.”

Sitting beside a pod-mate and talking it over is fine. Nobody has to.

Explaining vs. predicting

8:10 to 8:35

A rain dance and an umbrella

Two decision-makers (Kleinberg and coauthors):

  • one wonders whether to pay for a rain dance: a causal question, would acting change the outcome?
  • the other whether to carry an umbrella: a prediction, will it rain?

Different questions need different models (Shmueli).

Explain vs. predict

A model that explains A model that predicts
The question Why does this happen? What if we change something? Who, which, when, how many?
Judged by Whether it gets the cause right Whether it’s right about cases it hasn’t seen
Its variables Chosen by your model of the organization Whatever predicts, cause or not
On Pearl’s ladder Needs the second rung The first rung is enough

Fernhill asked a rain-dance question

Version 1: “Would replacing engineer-managers with professional managers, technical leads and AI raise delivery?”

That is a causal question. Its design, a before-and-after across all 120 teams, could support only an umbrella-grade answer: what changed.

The lot is what upgrades the claim. Each arm against its own past, assigned by lot: now “what if we change it?” has a fair comparison behind it.

The second rung of the ladder is a design, not an adjustment.

A predictive model of who leaves Riverbend

Live in Gemini, the prompt from the page:

Build a model that predicts left_org in staff_quarters from engagement (treat blanks as their own group), overtime_hours, caseload, tenure_years, training_completed, role, employment_type, pay_hourly, commute_miles, and site_id. Leave out S6’s rows for 2024Q3 and 2024Q4. Fit it on 2024 only and test it on 2025. In plain words: if I pick one person who left and one who stayed, how often does the model rank the leaver as riskier? Which predictors matter most?

What we found

  • It predicts moderately well: pick one person who left and one who stayed, and the model ranks the leaver as riskier about 7 times in 10. Fit on 2024 alone, it does just as well on 2025, a year it never saw. That is the umbrella test, and it passes.
  • Overtime alone does nearly as well (about 68 times in 100); engagement alone somewhat worse (about 64).
  • Commute distance predicts nothing: 11.5 miles against 11.2. A null finding is a finding.
  • One catch: every predictor was measured in the same quarter the person left. A list for the start of a quarter can only use what was known before it began.

Predictors that aren’t levers

A predictive model uses whatever predicts. That doesn’t make every predictor something a manager can pull.

  • Blank engagement predicts leaving. Making everyone fill in the survey won’t keep anyone.
  • Training completed is lower among leavers: 29% of their rows against 40% for stayers. Does training keep people? Name two other explanations before you say so.

A leaving model can decide whom to check in with next quarter, the umbrella. It can’t decide whether more training would keep people, the rain dance. That second question is Module 3’s.

The question sort

8:35 to 8:50 · the whole room · umbrella or rain dance

How the sort works

For each question, on a count of three, show a hand (or a colored card, or type U or R in the Meet chat):

  • Umbrella: it asks you to predict. Who, which, when, how many?
  • Rain dance: it asks you to explain and act. Why, or what happens if we change something?

One card belongs in both. Keep an eye out for it.

Card 1 of 9 · Nonprofit

Which donors are most likely to lapse next year?

Umbrella (predict). most likely. A ranked list is the whole answer. What would you do with the list?

Card 2 of 9 · Nonprofit

Would moving volunteer training online keep volunteers longer?

Rain dance (explain and act). Would moving … keep. It asks what happens if we change something, which a list of likely quitters can’t tell you.

Card 3 of 9 · Public

Which permit applications will take more than 60 days?

Umbrella (predict). Which. Flag them early. Nothing here says why they run long.

Card 4 of 9 · Public

Why do some districts close cases faster than others?

Rain dance (explain and act). Why. A why question wants a cause. Name two causes nobody could pull as a lever.

Card 5 of 9 · Private

Which subscribers will cancel this quarter?

Umbrella (predict). Which. A good umbrella. Blank survey answers may predict it, and that is allowed.

Card 6 of 9 · Private

Will a loyalty discount increase repeat purchases?

Rain dance (explain and act). Will … increase. The discount is the lever. Customers who get discounts may already be the loyal ones.

Card 7 of 9 · Fernhill

Which teams will deliver less than half their milestones next quarter?

Umbrella (predict). Which teams. A forecast of trouble spots. Fernhill could build it from the file as it stands.

Card 8 of 9 · Fernhill

Would giving every team a professional manager raise delivery?

Rain dance (explain and act). Would giving … raise. This is version 1’s own question. Its before-and-after design could show what changed, not what the change did.

Card 9 of 9 · Private

Which staff should managers check in with next quarter, and will the check-ins keep them?

Both. Which staff … and will the check-ins keep them. The first half is an umbrella and the second half is a rain dance. A prediction says where to act; a causal question says whether acting works.

What the sort showed

A prediction decides where to act, and a causal question decides whether acting works.

Many real decisions are like the last card. Thursday and Module 3 take up the second half.

Project workshop

8:50 to 9:40 · the Skeptic live, then your own Results

The Skeptic, live: what will it say?

The Skeptic gives up to four objections, each labeled:

  • unclear: the words allow more than one reading
  • unsupported: a claim with no reason or evidence
  • missing: something this kind of draft needs is absent
  • mismatched: two parts that do not fit together

Before we run it on Fernhill’s draft, write down the objections you expect.

The Skeptic, live

Fernhill’s version 1 Results draft, pasted into the Gem.

Compare what it says with what you predicted. For each objection, ask: does it follow from what the draft actually says?

What Fernhill changed

Over four runs, the author fixed what was fair:

  • Say what you measured. Ratings defined; “team-quarter ratings”; what each chart point is.
  • Say which summary the prediction meant. The average.
  • Give every finding a verdict and a rival. A honeymoon for ratings, AI alone for the median.
  • Back every “every” with a count. “94 of 120 teams”; the counts behind the easy and hard split.
  • Say where a claim comes from. The migration, every team from July 2025, and why it is the rival the file can test.
  • Check what would tell rivals apart. Ratings in each of the four quarters after.
  • Don’t take a side you can’t. Departures: “a cause of weak quarters or a result of the reorganization.”

And two it left alone

“If it lowered delivery…” was read as a causal claim. It is a conditional, a test of a rival (“If it lowered delivery, I would expect more work committed…”). The Skeptic’s own rule is not to attribute to the author a claim they did not make.

“…a result of the reorganization” was read as a causal claim. The sentence says departures “may be a cause of weak quarters or a result of the reorganization, and this file can’t tell which.” The hedge was dropped when the words were quoted.

Two readers of the same draft found different things. Telling a fair objection from an unfair one is the author’s job.

  1. The three notes on your chart (2 minutes): the question, the answer, the limit.
  2. Run the Skeptic (Course Skeptic Gem, Willamette account) on your Results draft so far. Say it is a Results draft.
  3. Use your revision memo as the filter: which objection would you act on, and which is unfair?
  4. Start section 5: what your finding does not establish.

Want a human reader? A neighbor, or your pod’s thread. Nobody has to.
